analysis.one_liner: Makes hours worked past 32 in a week overtime at time-and-a-half.
analysis.headline: The bill to shorten the standard workweek to 32 hours was introduced with one cosponsor, got a single committee hearing, and died without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal overtime law so that workers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act earn time-and-a-half pay after 32 hours in a week instead of 40, phased in over roughly four years (38 hours first, then 36, 34, and 32). It would also require time-and-a-half after 8 hours in a day, double time after 12, and would bar employers from cutting a worker's pay or benefits because the threshold dropped. It never advanced past a Senate committee hearing and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act who work more than 32 hours a week would either get overtime pay for those extra hours or see their schedules cut to 32 hours at the same weekly rate. Workers on long shifts would gain new daily overtime rights, and the bill explicitly forbids employers from slashing pay or benefits in response to the lower threshold.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly workers working more than 32 hours

how_it_helps.text: Workers would earn time-and-a-half for any week over 32 hours, phased in over four years (38 hours after the first period, then 36, 34, and finally 32), replacing the current 40-hour threshold.

The bill adds daily overtime on top of weekly overtime: time-and-a-half after 8 hours in a workday and double pay after 12 hours, so long shifts cost employers extra even if the weekly total is modest.
It includes an anti-cutback rule: employers may not reduce a worker's total weekly compensation rate or any benefit because the employee is newly covered by the lower overtime threshold.
It tightens overtime rules for hospital and health care employees on 14-day work schedules, ending much of the special flexibility those institutions currently have to avoid overtime pay.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of overtime-covered workers. Businesses whose employees routinely work 32 to 40 hours a week would owe time-and-a-half for that band, or would need to hire more staff and spread hours out. Hospitals and other 24/7 operations would face added overtime costs and scheduling changes. Some of these costs would likely be passed on to customers through prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers whose staff work over 32 hours

drawbacks.text: The bill raises labor costs for any employer whose workforce puts in standard 40-hour weeks, since hours 33 through 40 would newly command overtime pay — a steep, permanent increase in the cost of a normal week.

The wage protection only guarantees the hourly rate, not total earnings: an employer could respond by cutting a worker's schedule from 40 hours to 32, leaving that worker with a smaller paycheck than before even though the hourly rate is preserved.

Hospitals and nursing homes, which already struggle to staff 24/7 shifts, would lose the 14-day scheduling flexibility that currently lets them manage overtime exposure, potentially worsening staffing shortages or forcing higher prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who keep their full hours, this is a straight raise — time-and-a-half on hours 33 through 40 is a meaningful pay increase for tens of millions of people. The honest cost is that the mandate is expensive for employers, and the most predictable responses are hiring more part-time staff, cutting individual schedules toward 32 hours, raising prices, or automating — which is why the anti-cutback language matters but cannot force anyone to schedule 40 hours. The daily overtime provisions (8 and 12 hours) are the least controversial part; the 32-hour weekly threshold is a dramatic change to the baseline that every business in the country currently plans around. Whether the gains to workers outweigh the disruption depends heavily on how employers in each industry adjust, and the bill offers no cushion for small businesses.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee, which held one hearing, and it sat there with no vote until the congressional session ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the Thirty-Two Hour Workweek Act on March 14, 2024, joined by Sen. Laphonza Butler as its only cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, which Sanders chaired.
The committee held a single hearing on the bill, printed as S.Hrg. 118-329, but never took it up for a vote or reported it to the full Senate.
No further action was taken for the rest of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025, so the bill expired without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have owed overtime after 32 hours are better off, because the 40-hour overtime threshold stays in place and their labor costs are unchanged. Hourly workers hoping for either a four-day week or bigger paychecks for long weeks got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, who keep the 40-hour overtime line

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont and Chairman, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and oversaw a committee hearing on it

against.name: 49 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Offered no cosponsors, and the bill never moved beyond a hearing toward a committee or floor vote

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote during the two-year session

sides.party_line_note: Every bit of Senate support came from the sponsor, an Independent who caucuses with Democrats, and one Democrat; not a single Republican signed on, and the bill received no votes in committee or on the floor.

industries.industry: Retail, restaurants, and other large employers of hourly workers
industries.note: These businesses would owe time-and-a-half for every hour past 32 in a week — a large new cost on the most common full-time schedule. Their incentive to keep that cost off their books runs directly against the pay raise workers would otherwise get.

The bill narrows the special 14-day overtime rules hospitals rely on to staff round-the-clock shifts, likely raising their overtime costs. Those savings currently come at the expense of nurses and aides working long stretches without extra pay.
Employers facing a 32-hour overtime line would have strong demand for help splitting and spreading hours across more workers, a service the bill's own design would make newly necessary.
